# Exercises graded on a value instead of the exact code. Every exercise with a
# Submit button needs an entry here (and a -check chunk, which enables the button).
# The student's code and the -solution chunk are each run after the exercise's setup
# chunks, and the value from each is compared:
#   list(last_value = TRUE): the value of the last line (or the variable it assigns).
#     print(x) counts as x.
#   list(all_values = TRUE): the value of every bare line, in order.
#   list(var = ...): these variables, which the student's code must assign itself
#     (not just rely on setup).
#   list(expr = "..."): this Python expression, evaluated after the code runs (e.g. a
#     list the code changes in place).
#   defines = ...: variables the student's code must also assign (e.g. a saved result).
#   list(error = "TypeError"): the student's code must raise this error (no solution needed).
#   structure = ...: rules the code must also follow (see check_structure below), so
#     that e.g. typing the answer (True) doesn't pass a question about an operator.
# Strings, Booleans, types, lists vs tuples must match exactly; numbers must be close,
# and if the solution gives a float the student's answer has to be a float too.
# Any exercise not listed is graded by exact code match against its -solution chunk.
value_checks <- list(
  ex7 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex8 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex9 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex10 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex11 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex12 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex14 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex15 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex17 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  # Graded on the count, but starwars_species has to be saved too
  ex19 = list(last_value = TRUE, defines = "starwars_species", structure = "no_literal"),
  ex20 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex31 = list(last_value = TRUE, defines = "starwars_species_mass"),
  ex21 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex32 = list(last_value = TRUE, defines = "pivot_df"),
  ex23 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex24 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex26 = list(var = "starwars_big"),
  ex27 = list(var = "pilots_small"),
  ex28 = list(var = "starwars_pilots"),
  ex36 = list(last_value = TRUE, structure = "no_literal"),
  ex29 = list(last_value = TRUE),
  ex30 = list(last_value = TRUE)
)

# Python helpers for custom_checker (done in Python so they work the same on every
# Python version). Each run starts from a fresh namespace with only the exercise's
# setup chunks run in it, so the student's code and the solution can't affect each
# other (or leftovers from other exercises), even when the code changes data in place.
# get_result runs the code and returns the value being checked.
# check_structure returns "" if the code follows every rule, otherwise what is missing.
# raises says whether the code raises the named error.
# values_match compares a student's result to the expected one.
checker_py <- '
def fresh_namespace(setup):
    import builtins
    if setup is None:
        # Setup chunks unavailable, so fall back on a copy of what learnr just ran
        import __main__
        return dict(__main__.__dict__)
    g = {"__name__": "__main__", "__builtins__": builtins}
    for chunk in setup:
        exec(compile(chunk, "<setup>", "exec"), g)
    return g

def get_result(code, setup=None, var=None, expr=None, last_value=False, all_values=False, defines=()):
    import ast
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    if not tree.body:
        raise ValueError("no code")
    g = fresh_namespace(setup)
    values = []
    for stmt in tree.body:
        if isinstance(stmt, ast.Expr):
            node = stmt.value
            # print(x) shows the same thing as a bare x
            if (isinstance(node, ast.Call) and isinstance(node.func, ast.Name) and node.func.id == "print"
                    and len(node.args) == 1 and not node.keywords):
                node = node.args[0]
            values.append(eval(compile(ast.Expression(node), "<exercise>", "eval"), g))
        else:
            exec(compile(ast.Module([stmt], type_ignores=[]), "<exercise>", "exec"), g)
    # Variables have to be assigned by the student, not just left over from setup
    assigned = {n.id for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Name) and isinstance(n.ctx, ast.Store)}
    for name in defines:
        if name not in assigned or name not in g:
            raise NameError(name + " not defined")
    if expr is not None:
        return eval(expr, g)
    if all_values:
        if not values:
            raise ValueError("no values")
        return values
    if last_value:
        last = tree.body[-1]
        if isinstance(last, ast.Expr):
            return values[-1]
        if isinstance(last, ast.Assign) and len(last.targets) == 1 and isinstance(last.targets[0], ast.Name):
            # Last line is `name = expr`, so read `name`
            return g[last.targets[0].id]
        raise ValueError("last line is not an expression")
    names = [var] if isinstance(var, str) else list(var)
    for name in names:
        if name not in assigned or name not in g:
            raise NameError(name + " not defined")
    return g[var] if isinstance(var, str) else [g[name] for name in names]

def check_structure(code, rules=()):
    import ast
    tree = ast.parse(code)
    nodes = list(ast.walk(tree))
    for rule in rules:
        if rule == "compare":
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.Compare) for n in nodes):
                return "Make sure to use a comparison operator."
        elif rule in ("or", "and"):
            op = ast.Or if rule == "or" else ast.And
            if not any(isinstance(n, ast.BoolOp) and isinstance(n.op, op) for n in nodes):
                return "Make sure to use the `" + rule + "` operator."
        elif rule == "no_literal":
            last = tree.body[-1] if tree.body else None
            node = last.value if isinstance(last, ast.Expr) else None
            if isinstance(node, ast.Call) and isinstance(node.func, ast.Name) and node.func.id == "print" and len(node.args) == 1:
                node = node.args[0]
            if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp):
                node = node.operand
            if isinstance(node, ast.Constant):
                return "Use code to find the answer instead of typing it in."
        else:
            raise ValueError("unknown structure rule: " + rule)
    return ""

def raises(code, error, setup=None):
    import builtins
    g = fresh_namespace(setup)
    try:
        exec(compile(code, "<exercise>", "exec"), g)
    except getattr(builtins, error):
        return True
    except Exception:
        return False
    return False

def values_match(actual, expected):
    import math
    import numbers
    try:
        import numpy as np
    except ImportError:
        np = None
    try:
        import pandas as pd
    except ImportError:
        pd = None
    def is_bool(x):
        return isinstance(x, bool) or (np is not None and isinstance(x, np.bool_))
    def normalize(x):
        # values="name" and values=["name"] in a pivot table differ only by an extra
        # top level on the columns, and a one-column data frame holds the same values
        # as a series, so neither difference counts
        if isinstance(x, pd.DataFrame):
            if x.columns.nlevels > 1 and x.columns.get_level_values(0).nunique() == 1:
                x = x.droplevel(0, axis=1)
            if x.shape[1] == 1:
                x = x.iloc[:, 0]
        return x
    def match(a, e):
        # Data frames and series must have the same rows (in order), columns, and values;
        # names and dtypes (e.g. int vs float) are ignored
        if pd is not None and isinstance(e, (pd.Series, pd.DataFrame)):
            if not isinstance(a, (pd.Series, pd.DataFrame)):
                return False
            a, e = normalize(a), normalize(e)
            if type(a) is not type(e):
                return False
            try:
                if isinstance(e, pd.Series):
                    pd.testing.assert_series_equal(a, e, check_dtype=False, check_names=False, check_index_type=False)
                else:
                    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(a, e, check_dtype=False, check_names=False,
                                                  check_index_type=False, check_column_type=False)
                return True
            except Exception:
                return False
        if np is not None and isinstance(e, np.ndarray):
            if not isinstance(a, np.ndarray) or a.shape != e.shape:
                return False
            try:
                return bool(np.allclose(a, e, equal_nan=True))
            except TypeError:
                return bool(np.array_equal(a, e))
        # Lists and tuples have to be the same kind, with matching elements in order
        if isinstance(e, (list, tuple)):
            return type(a) is type(e) and len(a) == len(e) and all(match(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, e))
        if isinstance(e, dict):
            return isinstance(a, dict) and a.keys() == e.keys() and all(match(a[k], e[k]) for k in e)
        if isinstance(e, (set, frozenset)):
            return isinstance(a, (set, frozenset)) and a == e
        if isinstance(e, type):
            return a is e
        if is_bool(e):
            return is_bool(a) and bool(a) == bool(e)
        if isinstance(e, str):
            return isinstance(a, str) and a == e
        if isinstance(e, numbers.Number):
            if is_bool(a) or not isinstance(a, numbers.Number):
                return False
            # If the answer should be a float (e.g. from float()), an int does not count
            if not isinstance(e, numbers.Integral) and isinstance(a, numbers.Integral):
                return False
            return math.isclose(a, e, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9)
        try:
            return bool(a == e)
        except Exception:
            return False
    return match(actual, expected)
'

# Loads checker_py as its own Python module (so its functions can call each other)
load_checker_py <- function() {
  module <- reticulate::import("types", convert = FALSE)$ModuleType("lab_checker")
  reticulate::import_builtins(convert = FALSE)$exec(checker_py, module$`__dict__`)
  module
}

# The code of the setup chunks learnr ran before this exercise (following any
# exercise.setup chain), found on the learnr exercise that is calling the checker.
# NULL if it can't be found.
exercise_setup_code <- function() {
  for (frame in rev(sys.frames())) {
    ex <- get0("exercise", envir = frame, inherits = FALSE)
    if (is.list(ex) && !is.null(ex$chunks)) {
      chunks <- Filter(function(ch) !identical(ch$label, ex$label), ex$chunks)
      return(lapply(chunks, function(ch) paste(ch$code, collapse = "\n")))
    }
  }
  NULL
}

custom_checker <- function(label, user_code, solution_code, check_code, envir_result, evaluate_result, envir_prep, last_value, stage, ...) {
  # (learnr doesn't pass the last value of Python chunks, so we run the code)
  if (label %in% names(value_checks)) {
    spec <- value_checks[[label]]
    # Code that should raise an error is graded at the "error_check" stage, which
    # learnr runs instead of "check" when the student's code errors
    if (!(stage == "check" || (stage == "error_check" && !is.null(spec$error)))) return()
    setup <- exercise_setup_code()
    structure_msg <- tryCatch({
      helpers <- load_checker_py()
      reticulate::py_to_r(helpers$check_structure(user_code, as.list(spec$structure)))
    }, error = function(e) "")
    if (nzchar(structure_msg)) {
      return(list(message = paste(random_encouragement(), structure_msg), correct = FALSE))
    }
    correct <- tryCatch({
      helpers <- load_checker_py()
      if (!is.null(spec$error)) {
        isTRUE(reticulate::py_to_r(helpers$raises(user_code, spec$error, setup = setup)))
      } else {
        var <- if (length(spec$var) > 1) as.list(spec$var) else spec$var
        get_result <- function(code) {
          helpers$get_result(code, setup = setup, var = var, expr = spec$expr,
                             last_value = isTRUE(spec$last_value), all_values = isTRUE(spec$all_values),
                             defines = as.list(spec$defines))
        }
        actual <- get_result(user_code)
        expected <- get_result(solution_code)
        isTRUE(reticulate::py_to_r(helpers$values_match(actual, expected)))
      }
    }, error = function(e) FALSE)
    if (correct) {
      return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
    }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
  # Exact code checking (requires a <label>-solution chunk and <label>-code-check chunk)
  if (stage == "code_check") {
      if (user_code == solution_code){
          return(list(message = random_praise(), correct = TRUE))
      }
    return(list(message = random_encouragement(), correct = FALSE))
  }
}

gradethis_setup()
tutorial_options(exercise.completion = FALSE, exercise.checker = custom_checker, exercise.timelimit = 30, exercise.reveal_solution = FALSE)

## Goals

* To continue practicing with data frames, including their attributes, methods, and `pandas` functions. 
* To carry out basic exploratory data analysis with aggregation functions and `.groupby()`. 
* To examine relationships between variables using `pivot_table()`.
* To join data frames using `.merge()`.



## Introduction to DataFrames

One of the most commonly used collections of data in data science is the DataFrame. Let's do a quick introduction before we get into working with them.

### Different objects for different goals

There are different collections of data in Python because each works well in different contexts. We've already talked about lists and arrays:

Method 1: Lists (built-in to Python)

* Ordered and indexed
* Powerful built-in methods for sequences of data
* Flexible data types


Method 2: Arrays (must import `numpy`)

* All values of same data type
* Optimized for mathematical and matrix manipulations
* No row or column names

DataFrames two-dimensional tabular data structures that are especially useful if we have multiple observations of data of different types, or if we'd like for the data to be labeled.

Method 3: Data frames (must import `pandas`)

* Different columns can have different types
* Easy to manipulate by name
* Row and column names are built in
* Rows are "instances" as a `Series` object
* Columns are attributes of those individuals

## Setup

For this lab we will be using the `pandas` library in Python, as well as a new dataset containing information on various Star Wars characters from Episodes I-VII. We have several data frames to use as a part of the larger dataset--run the cell below to setup the environment.

## Data frame attributes

First, let's review some basic `pandas` using the `starwars` data frame. `starwars` includes the following variables:

* `name`: Name of the character
* `height`: Height (cm)
* `mass`: Weight (kg)
* `hair_color`, `skin_color`, `eye_color`: Hair, skin, and eye colors
* `birth_year`: Year born (BBY = Before Battle of Yavin)
* `sex`: The biological sex of the character, namely male, female, hermaphroditic, or none (as is the case for Droids)
* `gender`: The gender role or gender identity of the character as determined by their personality or the way they were programmed (as is the case for Droids)
* `homeworld`: Name of homeworld
* `species`: Name of species

## `.groupby()`

Now let's do some exploratory data analysis with `.groupby()` and our aggregation functions. 
Recall that the basic syntax is: `df.groupby("column_name")["value_column"].func()`.
We like to use the following functions:

* `.count()`: The number of observations 
* `.mean()`: The average of the observations
* `.min()`: The smallest observation
* `.max()`: The largest observation

Write a line of code to find out how many of each species there are in the data frame. Since everyone likely is labeled with a name, let's use `name` as the `value_column`.

## Pivot tables

Let's transition to working with pivot tables. 
Recall that when working with pivot tables we provide `DataFrame`, `index`, `columns`, `values`, and `aggfunc` arguments.

Write a line of code to count the number of characters with each eye and hair color combination. 
Eye color should be in the rows of your pivot table. Use "name" in the `values` argument.

```{python ex21, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}

```

```{python ex21-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
pd.pivot_table(starwars, index = ["eye_color"], columns = ["hair_color"], 
                        values = ["name"], aggfunc = "count")
```

```{r ex21-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```

```{r q22, echo=FALSE}
question("How many characters have black eyes and no hair?",
         answer("1.0"),
         answer("3.0"),
         answer("9.0", correct = TRUE),
         answer("`NaN`"),
         allow_retry = TRUE
         )
```

This is what is known as a "sparse" table--lots of categories with no values, and only a few with actual numbers. 
Let's assign our pivot table to a data frame called `pivot_df`, and use a method called `.stack()` on it.

```{python ex32, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}

```

```{python ex32-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
pivot_df = pd.pivot_table(starwars, index = ["eye_color"], columns = ["hair_color"], 
                        values = ["name"], aggfunc = "count")

pivot_df.stack()
```

```{r ex32-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Graded by custom_checker via value_checks (this chunk enables the Submit button)
```

This helped us a lot! It dropped all NaN values, and put it back in a tabular form.

## `.merge()`

Finally, let's consider `.merge()`. We have two variables in the `pilots` data frame--a string containing all vehicles a character has driven, and a string containing all starships a character has driven. 

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
vehicles_string <- rep(0, length(starwars$vehicles))

for (i in 1:length(starwars$vehicles)){
  vehicles_string[i] <- paste(unlist(starwars$vehicles[i]), collapse = ", ")
}

starships_string <- rep(0, length(starwars$starships))

for (i in 1:length(starwars$starships)){
  starships_string[i] <- paste(unlist(starwars$starships[i]), collapse = ", ")
}

pilots <- data.frame(cbind(starwars$name, vehicles_string, starships_string))
colnames(pilots) <- c("name", "vehicles", "starships")

write.csv(pilots, file = "/Users/amynussbaum/Documents/U of C/Courses/DATA119-Labs/dataframeslab/data/pilots.csv")
```

```{python ex_pilots, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}

```

Thus far, we have only shown you how to use `merge()` as a function. However, we can also use it as a method, where it acts on one of the data frames explicitly.

Now that we have learned how to join two data frames that have a column in common, let's take a look at how to add multiple data frames together when they all have the same columns. For example, we have seven smaller data frames containing all of the characters that appear in Episodes I-VII. 

```{python eps, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}
ep1 = pd.read_csv("./data/the_phantom_menace.csv", index_col = 0)
ep2 = pd.read_csv("./data/attack_of_the_clones.csv", index_col = 0)
ep3 = pd.read_csv("./data/revenge_of_the_sith.csv", index_col = 0)
ep4 = pd.read_csv("./data/a_new_hope.csv", index_col = 0)
ep5 = pd.read_csv("./data/the_empire_strikes_back.csv", index_col = 0)
ep6 = pd.read_csv("./data/return_of_the_jedi.csv", index_col = 0)
ep7 = pd.read_csv("./data/the_force_awakens.csv", index_col = 0)
```

Similarly to strings and lists, we can concatenate data frames together. The function to do so is `concat()`. `concat()` accepts a list of data frames to be concatenated. 

Concatenate the `ep1` and `ep2` data frames.

```{python ex29, exercise = TRUE, message = FALSE, exercise.setup = "setup_py"}

```

```{python ex29-solution, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
pd.concat([ep1, ep2])
```

```{r ex29-check, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}

```
